https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crl7.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, At least 53 people have been killed and some 5,000 displaced by the initial quake, which struck at a depth of just 15km By Lesthia Kertopati ,Â BBC News Indonesia Â and Â Gavin Butler Published 17 August 2026, 09:38 BST Updated 1 hour ago There are hundreds of disaster victims in Dampek village - but only one doctor. When a 7.7 magnitude earthquake struck the Indonesian island of Flores on Saturday, this area was among the worst-hit. Health facilities were toppled, electricity networks cut, and after two days aftershocks still rattled the makeshift shelters while inside, medical supplies rapidly diminished. "I am the only doctor here with hundreds of victims. I truly cannot cope," read an urgent appeal from Dr Melinda, the sole physician at the now-decimated Dampek Health Centre, on Sunday. "I have not had any rest since yesterday because casualties keep arriving around the clock." It is a problem that is playing out across Flores, as aid disruptions and ongoing tremors fuel fears among thousands of displaced survivors. Refugees are sleeping outdoors through sweltering days and frigid nights for fear that more buildings may collapse. Tents set up amid the rubble of collapsed hospitals are serving as makeshift emergency rooms for injured patients. And as landslides sever access roads and supplies dwindle in several parts of the island, there are growing concerns about how much longer survivors can hold out. At least 68 people have been killed and some 5,000 displaced by the earthquake, which struck shortly before 06:00 Saturday (23:00 GMT Friday) at a depth of just 15km. It is the country's deadliest quake since 2022, when hundreds of people were killed in West Java. Search-and-rescue teams and volunteers, including medical personnel, are continuing efforts to reach communities that were cut off by Saturday's quake, negotiating access roads that are scarred by landslides or choked with boulders. Dr Alhamzah, who works at Lalang Health Centre in East Manggarai, told the BBC on Monday that teams from regional hospitals were finally delivering much-needed assistance to places like Dampek - tending to severely injured patients with whatever resources they could muster. "If a patient's condition is critical, we will refer them to the hospital in Ruteng instead, which is about four hours away," he said. But Ruteng's hospital is also desperate for help. "We heard that medical assistance would be provided, but nothing has arrived yet," Rista Mari, a public relations officer at the Ruteng Regional General Hospital, told the BBC. "We hope that assistance will arrive soon." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Makeshift emergency rooms have been set up in tents after hospitals were destroyed in Saturday's devastating earthquake Early data from Indonesia's National Disaster Management Agency indicates that more than 1,000 houses were damaged by the earthquake, along with dozens of health facilities, schools and government offices. Medical teams are still working to determine the number of casualties, though - and the full scale of the disaster is still being uncovered. Indonesia is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity, lying along the meeting point of three major tectonic plates. In Flores' westernmost town of Labuan Bajo, the gateway to Komodo National Park and one of Indonesia's most popular tourist destinations, many survivors have been sleeping outdoors, fearful that if the tremors continue they might be crushed in their sleep. "The shaking was very scary. My house almost collapsed," said one farmer named Anastasia Imad, from a green emergency tent erected next to her damaged home. "We were worried that the aftershocks would collapse the house while we were sleeping." Herry Kabut, editor-in-chief of local publication Floresa Media, told the BBC that "each resident has set up their own evacuation post" amid blackouts, landslides and roadblocks. "So far, many basic necessities such as [basic foodstuffs] and clean water are in great demand," he said. "People have no idea where to evacuate. There's been no government advice. Many have fled to the hills and are starving." Health services across the island have similarly been forced to move outside and set up emergency tents due to damaged facilities. Ruteng Regional General Hospital's operating room, delivery room, pharmacy, and laboratory were all rendered defunct after the building's roof collapsed. Elsewhere, in Ngada Regency, local resident Charles Abar told the BBC that health facilities and equipment had been severely damaged and that, as of Sunday night, no medical assistance had arrived. He believes the government's response hasn't been swift enough. "I think facilities like emergency tents need to be provided immediately, but I also see that district and regional governments are struggling due to budget constraints, limited supplies, and so on," he said. Meanwhile, he added, villages have been cut off from aid and displaced people whose homes were damaged or destroyed have been forced to seek higher ground, as hundreds of aftershocks continue to rattle the island. "The community is still traumatised," he stressed. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Many displaced survivors are choosing to sleep outdoors amid fear of aftershocks and further building collapses Dr Alhamzah has taken to social media to appeal for support, seeking medical volunteers willing to travel to the disaster zone as well as donations of medicines and medical supplies. He has also warned that stocks of medicines at the disaster sites are running low. "People learned that doctors had arrived today, so many residents who had been sheltering in the hills came down," he explained. "As a result, we urgently need more medicines, as well as additional medical volunteers." On Sunday night, rescuers successfully reached a village on Palue Island, just north of Flores's mainland, that had been cut off for nearly two full days after the initial quake. Rescuers were only able to reach Nitung Village after a two-hour overland journey from the coast. "Our challenge was the road, which was still prone to landslides," said Sikka Deputy Police Chief Commissioner Marselus Yugo Amboro, who led the rescue mission. "It was a life-threatening route." Yugo said hundreds of homes in Nitung Village were severely damaged by the earthquake, and that residents had been sheltering in makeshift shelters. Electricity and communication lines were completely cut off following the earthquake, he added. "They haven't received aid yet because Nitung Village was isolated for nearly two days after the quake," he said, noting that efforts were underway to rush aid to the survivors. "This is likely the village in Sikka Regency that suffered the worst damage from the earthquake." https://www.dw.com/en/russians-on-the-go.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MOSm The Goethe-Institut in Moscow is one of three branches of Germany’s cultural center that'll have to close Image: Ramil Sitdikov/REUTERS Advertisement Germany's Goethe-Institut is set to close all Russian branches by Sunday, amid one of the worst spats in the history of relations between Russia and Germany . The Russian Foreign Ministry ordered the closure of the German cultural centers in Moscow , St. Petersburg, and Novosibirsk in response to Berlin's reaction to the attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in early August. The German authorities blamed Moscow for organizing the attack and announced sanctions. They include closing the Russian culture and education center in Berlin, known as the Russian House , and the Russian Consulate General in Bonn, as well tightening visa restrictions for Russian citizens. "All employees must cease their work in Russia as of September 13, 2026," Goethe-Institut Secretary General Gitte Zschoch said in a statement. "No more books can be borrowed from our libraries, and no further training can be offered. German language teachers are losing an important source of professional training and support. For people in Russia, this further restricts access to the German language, culture and reliable information from and about Germany." The library of the Goethe-Institut's Moscow branch won't be accessible anymore after September 13 either Image: Timur Gusarov/TASS/picture alliance DW asked its users in Russia to share how the closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect them personally. The responses received do not constitute a representative survey. All users shared their stories on conditions of anonymity. Russian authorities labeled DW an "undesirable organization" making every cooperation with the media company a criminal offense. 'We'll have to travel to another country' for German exams Many DW readers fear that, after the closure of the Goethe-Institut branches, they or their relatives will no longer be able to take exams in Russia for internationally recognized German language certificates. Some readers pointed out that closing the Goethe-Institut in Russia will hit ethnic Germans willing to relocate back to Germany, or late repatriates, especially hard. "I no longer live in Russia, having emigrated as a late repatriate, but my parents are still in Russia and were planning to take exams at the Goethe-Institut this fall or winter before submitting their resettlement documents. It looks like they'll have to take the exams in another country, which means additional stress and expenses for them," one reader said. DW also received responses from parents whose children are learning German and plan to continue their education in Germany. "My son attends a German school, and now we won't be able to take the exam in Russia. We'll have to travel to another country," one message said. Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video It remains unclear whether exams, language courses and educational programs will continue in Russia in another format or through partner organizations. Several readers expressed hope that at least some services will remain available online. Goethe-Institute closures hit teachers hard The closure of the institute will affect not only those planning to move to Germany or enroll at a German university. A German language teacher from the Moscow region told DW that her school had cooperated with the Goethe-Institut for more than 15 years. "This partnership was one of the most important pillars of our work. The institute supported us with high-quality teaching materials and provided modern books and publications about life in Germany, helping us make lessons engaging and relevant. Our students attended additional courses, and many successfully passed the Goethe certificate exams," she wrote. "I teach German and can't find a job in Russia," another teacher told DW. "It's terrible. I'm a German teacher, and I feel professionally stranded and lost," a third wrote. Despite the restrictions imposed since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine in 2022, demand for the institute's services remained high. According to the Goethe-Institut, around 10,000 people studied German through its programs and partnerships in 2025. Before 2023, that number used to stand at around 16,000 people. The institute administered roughly 22,000 exams, and its libraries were visited by 6,700 people in 2025. 'Culture has become a hostage to political decisions' Many readers perceive what is happening as another stage in the destruction of ties between Russia and Germany. "We would like cultural relations between the Russian Federation and Germany not to be destroyed," one DW user responded. "It is sad to realize that culture has become a hostage to political decisions. The closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect people who have no way of influencing politicians." Leipzig/Halle airport in Germany was the target of an attempted drone attack in August 2026 Image: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS Some DW readers from Russia specifically draw attention to the responsibility of politicians. One reader called the decision to close the institutes another step toward isolating the country and wondered why its consequences affect ordinary citizens rather than the Russian politicians who make such decisions. "Why can the people making decisions to isolate Russia from Europe simultaneously provide their own children and close relatives with a European education and a European way of life?" a DW user asked, proposing a ban on the education of the children and close relatives of members of Russia's top leadership at universities in Germany and other EU countries. Part of the audience considers Moscow's decision expected. "The closure of the branches looks like a logical response to the closure of the Russian House in Germany. Could it have been otherwise? It is a pity that cultural and humanitarian ties between the countries are becoming hostages to politics," one reader wrote. Some Russians hold Germany responsible for deteriorating relationship Some Russians however believe that closing the Goethe-Institut branches in Russia was the right step and blame Germany for the recent escalation of the conflict with Russia. "German authorities have buried cultural cooperation with Russia by shutting down the Russian House. The responsibility lies entirely with the German side, " said one of the survey participants. A bilateral intergovernmental agreement between Russia and Germany from 2011 regulates the work of the Russian House in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut's branches in Russia. It obliges both countries, on the basis of reciprocity, to ensure conditions necessary for the operation of their cultural centers. However, it does not in any way provide for the automatic closure of one country's cultural centers in response to the other country doing so. President of the Goethe-Institut Gesche Joost called the closure of its branches in Russia "the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations." According to its website, the Goethe-Institut has 154 branches in 100 countries. This number includes the three branches in Russia that are now being closed. https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/.text: Hurricane Isaias is in the Gulf of Mexico as the season's first Atlantic hurricane. It is projected to make landfall along the northern US Gulf coast as a category 2 hurricane. Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Hurricane Isaias is in the Gulf of Mexico as the season's first Atlantic hurricane. It is projected to make landfall along the northern US Gulf coast as a category 2 hurricane. Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty Images Hurricane Isaias Key things to know about Hurricane Isaias as millions under evacuation orders The hurricane is first in the Atlantic in what has turned into a very late season. Here’s what forecasters are saying about where Isaias will hit and how hard Maya Yang Fri 9 Oct 2026 21.50 EDT Last modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 21.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Hurricane Isaias, which made landfall on the US Gulf coast Friday night, was forecast to bring a dangerous storm surge, significant rainfall, flooding and strong winds across the US Gulf coast this weekend. Millions of people across several states, including Florida, Georgia and Alabama, were under evacuation orders as officials prepared for the storm. All three states issued states of emergency. The hurricane, the first in the Atlantic in what has turned into a very late 2026 season, made landfall as a category 2 storm, with sustained winds of 105 mph. The National Weather Service warned that Isaias could produce a “ life-threatening storm surge ” along parts of the northern Gulf coast, which occurs when rising ocean water moves inland from the coastline. 1. What are forecasters saying about where Isaias will hit and how hard? Isaias made landfall along the northern Gulf coast late Friday as a category 2 storm. The National Hurricane Center (NHC) warned it would bring a “life threatening” storm surge and “devastating winds likely across the Florida panhandle and Alabama coasts”. Isaias could bring 4-8in of rain, with locally higher totals up to 15in (380mm), across parts of the Gulf coast. Forecasters warned of significant flash and river flooding, especially in southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and south-western Georgia. Hurricane-force winds were expected to spread inland as far as 100 miles (160km) from the Alabama coast, the NHC said. There were also warnings of possible tornadoes late Friday or Saturday in its outer band of rains. The NHC said: “Across much of the remainder of the Southeast, rainfall amounts of 2 to 5 inches are expected. Localized higher amounts up to 10 inches are possible, especially across the Southern Appalachians and coastal Carolinas.” 2. What do the emergency response preparations look like? Florida , Georgia and Alabama have declared states of emergencies, with mandatory evacuations ordered in some coastal communities. Numerous evacuation shelters have opened across Florida, Louisiana, Alabama and Mississippi, with more than 370 trained American Red Cross (Arc) disaster workers supporting the response. The Arc is also pre-positioning cots, blankets, shelf-stable meals and other emergency supplies across the region. About 5,000 national guard troops were expected to mobilize in Florida, where at least four school districts cancelled late-week classes. Before the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the US. 3. How come this season’s first Atlantic hurricane is so late? Is El Niño a factor? The El Niño climate pattern is a factor in this year’s quieter Atlantic hurricane season . While it warms sea surface temperatures in the Pacific where storm activity has been greater, it also increases wind shear – changes in wind speed and direction with height – over the Atlantic, which can disrupt tropical storms before they strengthen into hurricanes. The hurricane season begins 1 June and runs up to the end of November with the height of the season usually from the middle of August to the middle of October. The last hurricane to make landfall in the US was Hurricane Milton, which came ashore near Florida’s Siesta Key on 9 October 2024. It followed Hurricane Helene a month earlier, which killed more than 250 people and was the deadliest hurricane to hit the mainland US since Hurricane Katrina in 20o5. 4. What are storm surges and where are they expected to hit? As a hurricane approaches a coast, the churning winds force ocean water up on to land; atmospheric pressure from the storm also helps squeeze the water ashore. The shallower the continental shelf, the higher the threat of a dangerous surge. The water may take a couple of days to fully subside. Storm surge was expected from south-east Louisiana to Suwannee, in north-east Florida, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa). Up to 9ft of storm surge is forecast between Dauphin Island, Alabama, and Indian Pass, Florida. chart 5. How ready are local officials and Fema? Although state officials have declared their preparedness, Isaias will be a key test of the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (Fema) ability to respond to a major hurricane after significant staffing cuts and an overhaul of the agency under the Trump administration. About 17% of Fema’s workforce left in fiscal year 2025, following Trump’s push to downsize the agency and shift more responsibility to states. The agency’s staffing reductions were not carried out systematically to ensure Fema could still meet its statutory obligations, said Chris Currie, director of homeland security and justice at the GAO. “It’s not whether Fema is going to respond. They’re going to respond. It’s more about the depth,” Currie said. Fema, however, said: “FEMA Incident Management Assistance Teams are deploying to Alabama and Florida, and FEMA personnel are embedded in state emergency operations centers. FEMA is also prepositioning emergency supplies at Maxwell air force base in Montgomery, Alabama, to supplement state resources if requested.” Explore more on these topics Hurricane Isaias Hurricanes Florida Alabama US weather Extreme weather Georgia news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://hungarytoday.hu/budapest-aiport-.text: Budapest Aiport Offers New Destinations for the Winter Season Even though Hungary is bidding farewell to the warm weather for now, the range of flight options remains diverse during the colder months. The winter flight schedule took effect on Sunday. More than 185 destinations are accessible from Liszt Ferenc Airport during the current winter season, including several new ones. Compared to last year’s winter flight schedule, travelers have 10% more bookable seats at their disposal. This is primarily due to an increase in flight frequencies on existing, high-demand routes, as the airport operator Budapest Airport announced in a press release. In the 2026/27 winter flight schedule, travelers to Asia will benefit from more frequent connections. Flights from Shanghai and Beijing to Budapest operate daily, and there are three direct flights per week between Guangzhou and the Hungarian capital. The expanded schedule also makes it easier to connect to several destinations in Southeast Asia with a layover. Guangzhou, China. Photo: Pixabay Flight frequencies have also been increased within Europe. This benefits travelers planning a short vacation, a city break, or a visit to the Christmas markets. Thirty five percent more seats are available to Scandinavia than last winter. Wizz Air now offers four flights per week to Oslo. Between Copenhagen and Budapest, SAS Scandinavian Airlines will operate two daily flights on several days in November and December. Copenhagen, Denmark. Photo: Pixabay Airlines are also expanding their capacity in other European markets: There are 50% more seats available to Poland, 7.4% more to the Baltic states, and 12% more to Spain than in the 2025 winter flight schedule. One of the new features of the winter flight schedule is the expansion of the route network to the United Kingdom. EasyJet is launching four new routes between Budapest and Belfast, Bristol, Liverpool, and London Southend. Clifton Suspension Bridge, Bristol, England. Photo: Pixabay The route to London Southend will be offered year-round. On the other three routes, two flights per week are scheduled between mid-November and the end of December. According to Budapest Airport, the number of routes served by EasyJet from Budapest has risen from three to eleven over the past three years. Marsa Alam in Egypt is also a new addition to Wizz Air’s route network. The resort is located on the west coast of the Red Sea and, in addition to its beaches, is known for its diving opportunities, diverse underwater world, and excursions into the desert. The new flight connection allows for direct travel to the Egyptian vacation destination even during the winter months.
